newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian dollar unstrung by rate rumours.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian dollar unstrung by rate rumours.

text.p: The Australian dollar was bundled lower Friday as bulls came unstrung over Asian selling and whispers of a possible cut in domestic interest rates.

The dollar had looked close to greater things this morning as samurai-related buying sent it surging to the stubborn US$0.7935 resistance level. But, as with every other occasion this week, it was pounced upon by sellers and battered back.

Some local banks joined the exodus, leading to dark rumours a domestic rate cut was in the air. "Certain banks, who are credited with having foreseen the July RBA cut, have been dumping the AUD and buying bill futures," said one dealer.
"People saw that, put two and two together, and came up with a 1/2 point cut," he said, only half joking.
By 5.00 pm (0700 GMT) the dollar fled to US$0.7995/00 from a US$0.7935 high and US$0.7932/37 late here Thursday.

Traders said good exporter bids were waiting at US$0.7890 which should cushion the currency near term, but a retreat to US$0.7850 was more than possible if Europe and New York took the rate rumours at all seriously.
The implications of the talk were even grimmer against the yen where the attraction of Australia's relatively high yields has been the dollar's single greatest asset this year.
Japanese retail investors, facing record low rates at home, have been pouring money into A$ dual currency samurai bonds which offer a far better return.

There was a pause after the July rate cut but issues began to reappear recently as soft Japanese economic data soothed fears of a rate hike. Three samurais had been launched this week, with another rumoured to have gone through this morning.

However, analysts were unsure if the attraction would survive another cut in domestic rates, which was why the market had reacted so defensively to talk the RBA could ease again at its monthly board meeting on Tuesday.
A Reuter survey of 35 economists on Friday found almost all expected no change in policy after the meeting, although a few thought a move was possible if unlikely.

"The next move will be down, but we think the RBA will want to see how the December round of enterprise wage bargaining progresses and how well the budget passes through the Senate, before taking the final decision," said Michael Thomas, an economist at CS First Boston Australia.
The RBA justified its last cut in part by pointing to a slowdown in wages growth, but cautioned that the easing process could be reversed if enterprise awards were to accelerate.
Last week's Federal Budget had promised a tightening in fiscal policy which was considered necessary to relieve pressure on national savings and the current account deficit.

But some savings measures were threatened by minor parties in the senate, where the government is two seats short of a majority, so analysts thought it possible the RBA would want to see how much of the budget passed before changing policy again.

Others, though, argued that all the reasons the bank cited in support of the last cut were just as valid today. "The RBA said the easing was insurance against a slowdown," said one. "Well you can never have enough insurance, can you?"
The RBA board meets Tuesday, so if it did decide to ease an announcement was likely Wednesday morning, analysts said.

Today's domestic data did nothing to clear the confusion. Building approvals for July rose 8.1 percent, twice what the market had been expecting, but that only corrected for a 7.9 percent dive in June and merely confirmed the housing market was bumping along the bottom, analysts said.
The local dollar faded to 85.57/67 yen from a 86.01 peak and 85.90/00 late here Thursday and slipped to 57.9 in trade weighted terms from a previous 58.1 close.
